title: Wrinkles and Magnetic Flux Trapping in Graphite Nanoflakes: A Possible Source and Manifestation of Room-Temperature Superconductivity
authors: Muhammad Saad, Sergey I. Nikitin, Dmitry A. Tayurskii, Roman V. Yusupov
abstract: The paper reports on a possible manifestation of local high-temperature superconductivity in graphite nanoflakes obtained from the bulk pyrolytic graphite by an extended grinding and subsequent annealing at 670 K in the air. Analysis of transmission electron microscopy (TEM) images shows that such treatment leads to a formation of high-density wrinkle-type defects at the basal-plane surface. The sample reveals the magnetic flux trapping - one of the key signatures of superconductivity - that persists up to 390 K and above. At the same time, both the as-ground (unannealed) and annealed in the vacuum samples manifest negligible flux trapping, and no wrinkles in their TEM images were found. The direct correlation between the appearance of high-density wrinkle arrays and the detection of the trapped magnetic flux above the room temperature strongly suggests that wrinkled regions serve a source of local high-temperature superconductivity in graphite.
summary: This experimental work proposes that wrinkles formed on the basal plane of graphite nanoflakes are the source of local high-temperature superconductivity. By comparing samples annealed in air versus vacuum, the authors found that air annealing creates these wrinkles, which are directly correlated with the detection of trapped magnetic flux persisting well above room temperature.
main_problem: The paper investigates the possibility that local high-temperature superconductivity can be induced in graphite nanoflakes.
main_result: The formation of high-density wrinkle-type defects on the basal plane, induced by air annealing, correlates strongly with the detection of trapped magnetic flux persisting above 390 K.
method: The study combines structural characterization using TEM/FFT and chemical analysis (XRD/XPS) with magnetic measurements (VSM) to correlate morphology changes with superconducting signatures.
model_or_system: The physical system is graphite nanoflakes derived from pyrolytic graphite, whose structure is manipulated by annealing in different atmospheres (vacuum vs. air). The key structural changes involve the transition from Moiré patterns to wrinkle arrays.
key_observables: Wrinkle-type defects, magnetic flux trapping (measured via ZFC/FC hysteresis loops), and the persistence of magnetic signals above room temperature.
important_parameters: Annealing temperature (670 K), magnetic field dependence, and the critical temperature range ($\geq 390$ K).
main_assumptions: The primary assumption is that the observed vertical shift in the magnetization hysteresis loop is due to trapped magnetic moments characteristic of superconductivity, and that the wrinkles are the structural source of this superconductivity.
figures_summary: Figures compare SEM/TEM images of as-prepared, vacuum-annealed, and air-annealed samples, showing the progression from Moiré fringes to wrinkles. Magnetization curves (ZFC/FC) are used to demonstrate the enhanced magnetic anomaly in the air-annealed state.
paper_structure: The paper follows a comparative experimental structure: first, characterizing the initial state (as-ground); second, analyzing the effect of vacuum annealing; and finally, detailing the crucial findings from air annealing, which links wrinkle formation to the superconducting magnetic signature.
why_interesting: Although focused on solid-state materials, the study explores how engineered structural defects (wrinkles) can induce emergent quantum phenomena (high-Tc superconductivity) in a layered material, which relates to understanding correlated electronic states in low-dimensional systems.
